arguments.title: The notion that Peter himself is the rock rather than his confession is first articulated by a bishop of Rome in the third century, a solitary view not even followed by all later bishops of Rome, and a late development in the West, never in the East

quotes.speaker: W. Robert Godfrey
quotes.work: How did the early church fathers interpret the “rock” of Matthew 16?
quotes.text: I would say, if this were the lightning round we could say, true. The notion that Peter himself was the rock rather than his confession being the rock seems first to be articulated by a bishop of Rome in the third century. Now, the third century is very early relative to us, but it's a long time after Jesus. Two hundred, two hundred and fifty years after Jesus. And this is a sort of solitary point of view of the Bishop of Rome initially, not even followed up by all later bishops of Rome in the ancient church period. So yes, I think generally speaking, the notion that Peter himself was the rock is a relatively late development in the Western church, never in the Eastern church, and in a later part of the ancient period. And many earlier interpreters would've seen that differently.

sections.text: Method v2 additions · 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4 · Sproul on the falling away and the man of sin
sections.primary: 2 Thessalonians 2:3–4 · Sproul on the falling away and the man of sin

arguments.title: Sproul reads 2 Thess 2:3: the day will not come unless the falling away comes first and the man of sin is revealed; he explains that an apostate is someone within the covenant community who repudiates a profession of faith, reports Benjamin Warfield's view that Paul means the first-century apostasy of the Jews, and goes on to «the man of sin, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God»

quotes.speaker: R. C. Sproul
quotes.work: The Antichrist: The Last Days According to Jesus with R.C. Sproul
quotes.text: That day will not come unless the falling away comes first. And now he's referring to an apostasy. That's what it means to fall away, a repudiation of true faith. Now remember the difference between paganism and apostasy. A pagan is one who is an unbeliever who has never made a profession of faith. An apostate is someone who makes a profession of faith and then later repudiates that profession of faith. That is, an apostate can only be someone who is within the covenant community, within the visible church. Benjamin Warfield is convinced that in this text Paul is not talking about an apostasy that will take place at the end of history in the manifestation of wickedness and moral decline within the Christian church. He's talking about the apostasy of the Jews in the first century, which was a major problem that is recounted in the New Testament. Christ came to His own, His own received Him not. Paul had this tremendous ongoing burden for his own kinsmen according to the flesh, Israel. The author of Hebrews warns that current generation of Jewish people about the dire danger of neglecting the great salvation that had come. And so the apostasy of the Jews or the apostasy of Israel is tied to that generation of Jews who rejected the Messiah that had appeared in their midst. And that would indicate a great falling away. But then Paul goes on to say, that day will not come unless the falling away comes first and the man of sin is revealed, the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above all that is called God or that is worship.

You see the word pastor, and that word is from the Greek word poimen, which means shepherd. We see that word being used in Ephesians 4 and elsewhere as the pastor teacher or shepherd teacher. And then we see in passages like Titus chapter 1, where Paul writes to Titus, this is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order and appoint elders in every town as I directed you. And the word elder there, as it's used in Titus and throughout the New Testament, is a word that is translating the Greek word presbyteros. Now, of course, you hear the word presbyteros and recognize that the cognate that we have for presbyteros in English is presbyter. We get Presbyterianism from that. And so presbyteros or presbuteroi in the plural are elders. And they are those who serve the church by ruling and

sections.text: Method v2 additions · Ephesians 4:8–11 · Reeder on Christ reigning over the church through gifts
sections.primary: Ephesians 4:8–11 · Reeder on Christ reigning over the church through gifts

arguments.title: Reeder says Christ reigns over the church from heaven by his position at the Father's right hand and functionally by his word and Spirit, and by giving: «he who descended is he who ascended and gave gifts to men», giving apostles for leadership in the official places of the church, pastors and teachers, and gifts to every member; he is also the head over his church, which he sends as the embassy of the kingdom

quotes.speaker: Harry Reeder
quotes.work: In What Way Is Christ Presently Reigning over the Church?
quotes.text: Well, he is in heaven, and he is reigning over the church by his position of authority, and that he has been placed at the right hand of the Father. And he is reigning over the church functionally by his word and with his spirit. So he has sent us the word of God, and he has sent us the spirit of God, and he is reigning through that. Secondly, he is reigning by his benevolent leadership of giving. The Bible says, he who descended is he who ascended and gave gifts to men. So he is reigning through giving apostles, that's men for leadership in the official places of the church. He is giving women and their giftedness to the church. So he gives people to the church. He gives ministries to the church, pastors, teachers, et cetera. And he also gives gifts to every single member of the church. So everyone is gifted by the Holy Spirit with their spiritual gift. There are ministries that Christ has established in his church and given to the church. And there are people that he has saved and gives them to the church. They were baptized and added to the church. So they are a part of the living stones that make up the New Testament temple of God. And so he's ruling and reigning. Secondly, he is the head over his church, and now he is sending his church as the embassy of the kingdom of God to extend the kingdom of God into this world.

sections.text: Method v2 additions · Matthew 13:24–30 · Cooper on the visible and the invisible church
sections.primary: Matthew 13:24–30 · Cooper on the visible and the invisible church

arguments.title: Cooper says not everyone who seems to be a member of God's church actually is: the visible church comprises all who claim to follow Christ, the invisible church all who really do; he retells Jesus's parable in Matt 13 of the wheat and the weeds, the enemy who sowed them and the master's order to let both grow together until the harvest

quotes.speaker: Barry Cooper
quotes.text: Not everyone who identifies as a member of the media is actually a member of the media and in the same way not everyone who seems to be a member of God's church is actually a member of God's church. That's what we mean by the visible and invisible church. The visible church comprises all those who claim to be or identify as followers of Christ. The invisible church comprises all those who really are followers of Christ. Jesus tells a story about this in Matthew chapter 13. A man sows good seed in his field and his servants are perplexed when the field turns out to have weeds in it as well as wheat. We thought you only sowed wheat. What's with all the weeds? The master says rather ominously, an enemy has done this. So what would you like us to do, say the servants. Shall we go and root up all the weeds? No, says the master. If you do that, you might accidentally root up the good stuff. Let them both grow together. I will separate them once and for all when the time comes for the harvest. The thing about wheat and weeds, as I discovered in the mid-1980s during a short-lived stint as a gardener is that it isn't always easy to spot the difference between a weed and a prize-winning flower. Some of the most destructive weeds look beautiful, and some plants which look very unprepossessing in their early stages grow up to be the most stunning orchids. You really need an expert gardener to know the difference.

sections.text: Method v2 additions · Ephesians 5 · Ferguson on the church as the bride of Christ
sections.primary: Ephesians 5 · Ferguson on the church as the bride of Christ

arguments.title: Ferguson says the picture of a faithful God and the church as his bride comes to its fulfilment in Jesus: the church is the bride of Christ, and Paul says in Ephesians 5 that this picture is embedded in the original creation of man and woman, marriage in Eden and ours being a picture of Christ and his people; Paul says the church will one day be presented in splendor, without spot or wrinkle, holy and without blemish

quotes.speaker: Sinclair B. Ferguson
quotes.outlet: Things Unseen with Sinclair B. Ferguson
quotes.text: That picture of a faithful, faithful God and the church as that God's bride comes to its fulfillment, of course, in the Lord Jesus. The church is the bride of Christ. And you remember that Paul says in Ephesians 5 that this picture is actually embedded in the original creation of man as male and female, a man and a woman, made for each other. That marriage in Eden, and our marriage too, is intended to be a picture of the relationship between the Lord Jesus and His people. It's a picture of His amazing love for us. As the hymn puts it, from heaven he came and sought us to be his precious bride. With his own blood he bought us, and for our life he died. And this is a picture that has many lessons to teach us. But here's one of the most important. Paul says that one day the church will be presented to the Lord in splendor, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, that she might be holy and without blemish. Think about that when you reflect on your own church fellowship.

sections.text: Method v2 additions · Christ the head of the body · Ferguson on Jesus as head of the church (Ephesians 4:15–16)
sections.primary: Christ the head of the body · Ferguson on Jesus as head of the church

arguments.title: Ferguson says that, in Paul's picture of the church as the body of Christ, the first lesson is that the Lord Jesus is the head of the body: he directs it, owns it, is its Lord; «it's Jesus' church, not my church or the minister's church»; and he recalls Paul in Ephesians 4:15–16: we grow up into Christ the head, joined and held together by every joint, when each part is working properly the body builds itself up in love

quotes.speaker: Sinclair B. Ferguson
quotes.outlet: Things Unseen with Sinclair B. Ferguson
quotes.text: First of all, the Lord Jesus is the head of the body. That is to say, he directs it. He owns it. He is the Lord of the body. It's Jesus' church, not my church or the minister's church. It's not even our church. It's his church. We need to remember that because often when things go wrong in churches, it's because we've forgotten this. So in all we do, and those who are elders or have spiritual oversight in any way, need to put this at the top of the agenda sheet. Jesus is head. It's His church, not ours. Another thing that's important in this picture is it reminds us that the members of the body are all different, but each member has a part to play, and they're all needed if the body is to function properly. Remember how Paul puts it in Ephesians 4, 15 to 16. He says, we grow up into Christ the head, joined and held together by every joint with which he equips the body, when each part is working properly. Then, only when each part is working properly, the body builds itself up in love. What a marvelous picture that is for us to understand how much we all need each other

sections.text: Method v2 additions · Matthew 28:18–20 · Tweeddale on the authority Christ delegates to those who minister in his name
sections.primary: Matthew 28:18–20 · Tweeddale on the authority Christ delegates to those who minister in his name

arguments.title: Tweeddale says the most important phrase of the Great Commission is «all authority in heaven and earth has been given to me» (Matt 28); Reformed theologians distinguish Christ's universal authority as eternal Son and Lord of creation, which he has not delegated to us, from his mediatorial authority over the church, which is the authority of Matt 28, delegated to those who minister in his name: they preach the word, pray, read Scripture and call for repentance

quotes.speaker: John Tweeddale
quotes.work: Do Christians Have Authority Over Sickness?
quotes.text: The most important phrase in the Great Commission comes in Matthew 28, 17, where Jesus says, All authority in heaven and earth has been given to me. Now, throughout the history of the Church, Reformed theologians have distinguished Christ's authority in two ways. On the one hand, they talk about Christ's universal authority as the eternal Son, as the second person of the Trinity, as the Lord of creation, as the creator and sustainer of all things. And in that sense, Christ is Lord over the universe, over the seas, over healings in our body and of sickness. And Christ at times has healed, but the ordinary affairs of life would lead us to believe that most of the time, the wages of sin is death and death is a natural part of the fallen world. And so Jesus is governor of the heaven and earth, but he has not delegated that authority to us. The second kind of authority we have is Jesus's mediatorial authority. That's the authority he has over the church, and that's the authority Jesus speaks about in Matthew 28. So he delegates his authority to those who minister in his name. So we preach the word. We pray down heaven. We read scripture. We call for repentance.

sections.text: Method v2 additions · 1 Corinthians 12:12 and Romans 12:4–5 · Waters on the unity of the body of Christ
sections.primary: 1 Corinthians 12:12 and Romans 12:4–5 · Waters on the unity of the body of Christ

arguments.title: Waters says that in Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12 Paul speaks of the church as body and that one concern is the unity of the body: Rom 12:4–5, «one body in Christ, though we are many», and 1 Cor 12:12, «just as the body is one and has many members, all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ»; Paul gives this unity as a given, a fact, not an exhortation to pursue it

quotes.speaker: Guy Waters
quotes.work: The Church and the Christian Life
quotes.text: And in Romans 12 and 1 Corinthians 12, he speaks of the church as body. And two things, I think, emerge from Paul's discussion of the church as body in these chapters. One concern for Paul is that believers understand the unity of the body. Romans 12, 4, one body. The very next verse, one body in Christ, though we are many, we are one body in Christ. 1 Corinthians 12, at the 12th verse, just as the body is one and has many members, All the members of the body, though many, are one body. So it is with Christ. Now notice when Paul talks about the unity of the body, he doesn't here give it as an exhortation. Pursue a unity that you don't have. Rather, it is a given. It is a fact. Paul says you are one in Christ. And that has implications, of course, for the way we're to live. It's telling that Paul tells churches that are racked by division and faction that they are one.

sections.text: Method v2 additions · Ephesians 2:20 · Cooper on the foundation of the apostles (no further apostles)
sections.primary: Ephesians 2:20 · Cooper on the foundation of the apostles

arguments.title: Cooper says Paul writes in Ephesians 2 that the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself the cornerstone, and that a foundation is laid only once: after the first-century apostles laid it and died there can be no further apostles in that sense, which is why the written testimony of the apostles and of those endorsed by them is uniquely authoritative today, with the authority to speak on behalf of Christ

quotes.speaker: Barry Cooper
quotes.text: In Ephesians chapter 2, Paul writes that the church is built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone. That view of the apostles as being included in the foundation of the Christian faith is crucial to understand because a foundation is laid only once. So after those apostles laid the foundation in the first century and then eventually died, there could be, by definition, no further apostles. No one subsequently could truthfully claim to be an apostle in the sense Paul talks about in Ephesians, because they would not be first-hand witnesses of the risen Lord Jesus, as the apostles were. Nor would they have received the visible endorsement of those first century apostles. That's one of the reasons why the written testimony of the apostles in the New Testament, and the New Testament writings of those specifically endorsed by the apostles, is so uniquely authoritative today. In the Roman Empire, an apostolos, from which we get the English word apostle, was anyone with the authority to speak to others on behalf of the emperor. Such was their authority that if you disobeyed them, it was as if you were disobeying the emperor himself. That's the kind of authority that the apostles' written testimony has. They have the authority to speak to us on behalf of, and with
